questions.prompt: Acetone (nail-polish remover) melts at −95 °C and boils at 56 °C. What is its state at 70 °C?
questions.explanation: 70 °C is above the boiling point (56 °C), so acetone is a gas. It would be a liquid only between −95 °C and 56 °C.

questions.prompt: Which changes of state **take in** energy from the surroundings? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: Melting, boiling (and evaporation) and sublimation need energy to overcome the forces between particles. Freezing and condensation give energy out as the particles come closer together.

questions.prompt: Water boils at a lower temperature in Kigali than at the seaside in Mombasa.
questions.explanation: Kigali is about 1 500 m above sea level, where air pressure is lower, so water boils at about 95 °C instead of 100 °C.

questions.prompt: In Musanze, water boils at about 94 °C. A pot of water at 22 °C is heated and its temperature rises by 4 °C every minute. How many minutes does it take to start boiling?
What is the name of the change when a solid turns directly into a gas without melting first?
questions.explanation: This is **sublimation**. Iodine crystals and moth balls (naphthalene) sublime when warmed.

questions.prompt: A student heats ice steadily. The thermometer stays at 0 °C while the ice is melting, even though heating continues. Use the particle model to explain why.
questions.marking_guide: 1 mark: the energy supplied is used to overcome (break) the forces of attraction between the particles. 1 mark: the particles do not move faster (their kinetic energy does not increase), so the temperature does not rise. 1 mark: the particles change from vibrating in fixed positions (regular arrangement) to sliding past each other; once all the ice has melted the temperature rises again.
questions.explanation: During a change of state, the energy goes into separating the particles rather than speeding them up, so the temperature stays constant until melting is complete.
